subtitle: Nominal style in three moves, and official letters unpacked
words.intro: A German parking fine is a small masterpiece. It knows the minute, the street, the paragraph and the sum, and it knows the difference between a warning and a fine. One sentence is all it takes, and it won’t have one person in it.

grammar[0].fact: The rule goes: take the verb out and make it a noun, then add a weak verb such as *erfolgen*. *Die Zahlung erfolgt*, the payment takes place. You’ve said nothing, and it’s taken a line. German writing guides have been complaining about this since at least the 19th century.

grammar[1].fact: German law also requires an official notice to say how you may object, in a passage called the *Rechtsbehelfsbelehrung*. It’s a long word that has saved a lot of people a lot of money: if it’s missing, you get a whole year to object rather than the usual month.

document.intro: A real yellow envelope. Every German knows this colour, and every German’s heart beats faster when one is in the letterbox. The postman writes the date on it by hand, and from that moment the clock is running. Look at the top: *Umschlag bitte aufbewahren*.
document.fact: This envelope is proof that you got the letter, even if you never opened it. Being on holiday is rarely an excuse.
reading.intro: Max parked outside the bakery for three minutes. On his windscreen he found a ticket for ten euros. He has decided to object, in writing, on principle, like Frau Huber. Here’s the correspondence.

reading.fact: A low parking warning is usually paid and done. Once you contest it, however, it can become a real procedure with its own fees, so a very small fine can grow.
